entities.name: Adam Stanisław Krasiński
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adam Stanisław Krasiński (1810–1891) was a Polish Catholic bishop who served as Bishop of Vilnius (Wilno) and played a significant role in the complex politics of Polish Catholic identity under Russian imperial rule. Born into the Polish nobility, he was a member of the distinguished Krasiński family that had produced major literary figures including the Romantic poet Zygmunt Krasiński.

Krasiński was appointed Bishop of Vilnius in 1858 and navigated the increasingly difficult situation of Polish Catholicism under Russian pressure. When the January Uprising of 1863 broke out, he faced an impossible dilemma: explicit support for the insurrection would lead to his arrest, while total passivity would be seen as abandonment of his flock. His position during the uprising was ambiguous—he was eventually exiled by the Russian authorities to Viatka in 1863, where he remained under house arrest until 1883.

His two-decade exile became a defining symbol of Russian religious persecution of Polish Catholicism. The suppression of his diocese, the deportation of clergy, and the forced Russification of Catholic religious practice in the Vilnius region defined the conditions of Polish Catholic existence for a generation. Krasiński's eventual return and his continued episcopal witness within these constraints made him a figure of quiet but significant resistance in the history of Polish religious freedom.
